passage:
Rain hammered the bus-stop roof, and the school bus was already twenty minutes late. Tanvir kicked a puddle.
"At my old school the bus was never late," Tanvir told Damini, the girl from the new class who shared the shelter. "And everybody was friends. Nobody ever fought."
Damini shrugged. "Nobody?"
"Nobody. It was the best class in the world."
While digging for a dry handkerchief, Tanvir pulled out an old rough notebook. On the back page, in big angry letters: NEVER SHARING MY TIFFIN WITH THAT BENCH AGAIN!! Below it was a drawing of a cross face.
Tanvir stared at it, then quickly shut the notebook. "That was just one day," Tanvir mumbled, as the bus splashed round the corner.

qa.q: What was written on the back page of Tanvir's old notebook?
qa.a: NEVER SHARING MY TIFFIN WITH THAT BENCH AGAIN!!, with a drawing of a cross face below it.

qa.q: Why does Tanvir insist the old class never fought?
qa.a: Tanvir misses the old school and feels unsettled in the new one, so from far away the old class feels perfect and the quarrels have faded.

qa.q: How could a parent help Tanvir without arguing?
qa.a: They could say it's fine to miss old friends, then ask about an ordinary day there, good and grumpy bits, and about one nice thing in the new class. 🙂

qa.q: How might Damini feel hearing that the old class was the best in the world?
qa.a: Damini might feel the new class is being compared unfairly, or that Tanvir isn't ready to give it a chance yet.

grounding: A child who changed schools calls the old class perfect until an angry note in an old notebook shows the forgotten quarrels.

passage:
Vinita pressed her forehead against the balcony grille of their new flat in Bengaluru, watching the colony kids play cricket below.
"In Kolkata, my class was like a family," she said. "We did everything together. Sports day, tiffin, everything."
Her little brother Tejas looked up from his jigsaw. "You cried about Mouli every week. She said your drawing was ugly."
"That never happened."
"And the time the whole class blamed you for the broken window."
Vinita opened her mouth, then closed it. She did remember the window, a little: standing alone by the staff room, cheeks hot.
"It was still nice," she said, quieter.
"Some of it," Tejas agreed, and fitted in a piece.
Downstairs, a girl waved up at the balcony. Vinita hesitated, then waved back.

qa.q: Which city did Vinita's family move from?
qa.a: Kolkata; they now live in a new flat in Bengaluru.

qa.q: What does Vinita's quieter 'It was still nice' suggest she is feeling?
qa.a: Vinita feels wistful and homesick for her old class, but she is starting to recall the hard moments too and admit it wasn't perfect.

qa.q: What could help Vinita settle into the colony?
qa.a: Saying yes to small chances like the girl's wave, and letting herself miss Kolkata while giving new friends a fair try.

qa.q: How does Tejas see his sister's story about Kolkata?
qa.a: Tejas remembers the weekly tears and the window blame, so to him 'like a family' leaves a lot out.

grounding: A girl who moved cities remembers her old class as a family, and her brother reminds her of quarrels she has smoothed away.

passage:
"Uma Didi, my old school had the best teacher in the world."
"Better than Mrs Rao here?"
"Way better. Miss never shouted."
"Pankaj, you told me on the phone last year she made you stand outside for talking."
"That was only once. Maybe twice."
"And the football team? You said they never passed to you."
"They passed sometimes." Pankaj pulled at a thread on the sofa cushion. "It just feels like everything was nicer there."
"It feels like that because you miss it. Missing something is allowed."
"Then why do I only remember good stuff?"
"Because far-away things look smooth. Like hills from the train window, all soft and green. Up close there are rocks."
"Mrs Rao let me feed the class fish today."
"See? A rock and a fish."

qa.q: What did Mrs Rao let Pankaj do today?
qa.a: Mrs Rao let Pankaj feed the class fish.

qa.q: Why does Pankaj remember only good things about the old school?
qa.a: Pankaj feels homesick for the old school, so bad days like standing outside or not getting passes have faded, and the old place feels nicer than it was.

qa.q: Which part of Uma's reply helped, and why?
qa.a: Uma said missing it was allowed before mentioning the rocks, so Pankaj didn't feel scolded and could admit the new school has good moments too.

qa.q: If you were Uma, what would you hope Pankaj notices next week?
qa.a: More good moments at the new school, like the fish, instead of only comparing it with a smoothed-out memory. 🙂

grounding: A child who changed schools praises the old teacher and team, while an older cousin gently recalls the quarrels and slights now forgotten.

passage: When we moved to Pune, I told everyone my old class in Bhopal was the best class in the whole world. Nobody fought. Everybody shared tiffin. The teacher smiled all day. Then Gautam, my old bench partner, did a video call. I said, "I miss our class so much." He said, "Me too. Remember when you and Rohit didn't talk for a whole month? And you cried because someone spilled ink on your chart?" I stopped. I had forgotten all of that. It was like the fights had fallen out of my head. My new class is a bit noisy. Maybe my old one was too. I'm Jaya, and I still miss it, but maybe not every part.

qa.q: Who did Jaya not talk to for a whole month in the old class?
qa.a: Rohit.

qa.q: Why did Jaya stop when Gautam mentioned the fights?
qa.a: Jaya was surprised, because those quarrels had slipped out of memory and the old class had felt perfect.

qa.q: What could Jaya try now that the old class doesn't look quite so perfect?
qa.a: Jaya could give the noisy new class a fair chance, since the old one had its hard days too.

qa.q: What might Gautam feel when Jaya says the old class was perfect?
qa.a: Gautam misses Jaya too, but remembers the real class with its fights and tears, so he gently brings back the rough parts.

grounding: A child who moved schools remembers the old class as perfect until a friend reminds them of the quarrels.

passage: Teacher's note, Class 3C, Wednesday. Farhan joined us from a school in Lucknow three weeks ago. He is polite and bright, but most days he tells the class that in his old school "nobody ever fought," "the teacher gave stars every day," and "everyone was my best friend." Today, when two boys argued over a football, he said loudly, "This never happened in my old school." Some children felt hurt. At pickup I spoke with his mother. She smiled and said he used to come home upset about a boy who took his tiffin, and once begged not to go back. I think he misses it so much that the hard days have faded. Tomorrow I'll pair him with Kabeer for class jobs and ask him to draw his old school and his new one side by side. — Mr Naveen

qa.q: Which city did Farhan's old school sit in?
qa.a: Lucknow.

qa.q: Why might Farhan believe nobody ever fought in his old school?
qa.a: He misses it a lot, so the good parts feel bright while the hard days, like the tiffin trouble, have quietly faded from his mind.

qa.q: What next step did Mr Naveen choose, and how might it help Farhan settle?
qa.a: Pairing him with Kabeer for class jobs and drawing both schools side by side, so he builds new friendships and sees both places more fairly.

qa.q: How might the other children in 3C feel when Farhan praises his old school?
qa.a: Some feel hurt or compared unfairly, as if their class isn't good enough, which could make it harder for them to welcome him.

grounding: A teacher notices a child who moved schools praising his old class as perfect while forgetting the quarrels he once had there.

passage: It rained all morning, so recess at Keerthana's new school in Bengaluru happened inside, in a hot, noisy classroom. Keerthana sat by the window while the others played a clapping game she did not know. When Reena came over, Keerthana said, "In my old school in Coimbatore, nobody ever fought. We all shared everything." Reena nodded. "Even the swing?" Keerthana opened her mouth, then shut it. There had been a swing, and there had been Abinaya, who never let anyone else on it, and that one day Keerthana cried behind the water tank. "Well," she said slowly, "mostly." She still missed the old classroom with the fan that squeaked. But she let Reena teach her the first clap.

qa.q: Why did recess happen inside the classroom?
qa.a: Because it rained all morning.

qa.q: Why does Keerthana feel lonely and remember her old school as perfect?
qa.a: She feels left out while the others play a game she does not know, so the old school, where she belonged, seems warm and free of fights.

qa.q: What could help Keerthana settle into the new class?
qa.a: She could keep saying yes to small invitations like Reena's clapping game, and remember that her old class also had hard days.

qa.q: How might Reena feel when Keerthana says nobody ever fought at the old school?
qa.a: Reena might feel a little doubtful, and maybe worried that the new class seems worse to Keerthana, which could be why she comes over to include her.

grounding: Shows a child who has moved schools picturing the old class as perfect until a question brings back a forgotten quarrel.

passage: Darshan pushed his dal around the plate in their new flat in Thane. "At my Nashik school everyone was my friend," he told his big sister, Sarita. "Here nobody even says hi." Sarita raised an eyebrow. "Everyone? What about Ronak, who ate your tiffin every single day?" "That was only once." "You came home crying about it every week, Darshan. Aai had to write a note to the teacher." Darshan frowned. He could see the old classroom clearly: the mango tree outside, his seat by the door, the drawing of the tiger he made. Ronak was blurry, like a smudge on a photograph. "Maybe twice," he said. Sarita smiled and passed him the papad. "You'll have new tigers to draw here too." Darshan did not answer, but he ate the papad.

qa.q: Who used to eat Darshan's tiffin at the Nashik school?
qa.a: Ronak ate Darshan's tiffin.

qa.q: Why does Darshan honestly think the tiffin trouble happened only once?
qa.a: He misses his old school and feels sad in the new flat, so the happy parts like the mango tree and the tiger drawing feel clear while the upsetting parts have gone blurry.

qa.q: How could Sarita help Darshan without making him feel silly?
qa.a: She could agree that he misses the old school and then ask what he would like to find at the new one, like a place to draw 🙂

qa.q: How does Sarita see Darshan's picture of the old school?
qa.a: Sarita remembers the weekly crying and Aai's note, so she sees that his memory has smoothed the hard parts away and gently wants him to see the whole picture.

grounding: Shows a child in a new city remembering the old class as all friendship while forgetting the repeated tiffin trouble.

passage:
"Vijay bhaiya, my old school had the best library in the world."
"The one with six shelves?"
"It had the best books. And Mrs Dsouza read to us every Friday."
"You told me she shouted when you dropped the atlas."
"She didn't shout. She just said it loudly."
Vijay laughed. "Nandini, you hated that library for a whole month."
"No I didn't."
"You said the dust made you sneeze and the big boys hid the comics."
Nandini hugged her knees on the sofa. "It was still better than here. Here I don't know where anything is."
"Ah." Vijay sat down beside her. "So the new library is hard because it's new."
"Maybe."
"Want to go on Saturday and find the comics together?"
Nandini shrugged, but she was already thinking about which shelf they would be on.

qa.q: Who read to the class every Friday at Nandini's old school?
qa.a: Mrs Dsouza read to them every Friday.

qa.q: What does Nandini's hugging her knees suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: She feels lost and a bit lonely in the new library, so the old one seems perfect because she knew where everything was there.

qa.q: Which part of Vijay's approach works, and why?
qa.a: Offering to visit the new library with her on Saturday works better than only correcting her memory, because it tackles the real problem of feeling lost.

qa.q: How might Vijay see Nandini's memory of the old library?
qa.a: Vijay sees that she is leaving out the dust, the hidden comics and the loud teacher, but he also understands she is uneasy about the new school.

grounding: Shows a child calling the old school library the best while forgetting the troubles she once complained about.

passage:
My old school in Lucknow was the best. My class was so fun, and everyone was my friend. The teacher gave us toffees on Fridays.

At my new school in Bhopal, nobody sits with me at lunch yet, and the teacher is strict.

Yesterday I told my cousin Vinita, "My old class never fought."

Vinita laughed. "Samir, you cried every week about Rehan taking your pencil box. And you hated the Friday tests."

I forgot about Rehan. And the tests.

Maybe my old class wasn't perfect. Maybe it just feels perfect because it's far away now.

qa.q: What did the teacher at the old school give on Fridays?
qa.a: Toffees.

qa.q: Why does Samir remember the old class as perfect?
qa.a: Samir feels lonely at the new school, so the old class feels warm and perfect, and the quarrels have faded.

qa.q: What could help Samir feel better at the new school?
qa.a: Samir could try sitting with one new classmate at lunch, and remember the old school had hard days too.

qa.q: How does Vinita see Samir's memory of the old class?
qa.a: Vinita finds it funny and remembers the pencil-box quarrels and Friday tests that Samir forgot.

grounding: A child who has moved schools remembers the old class as perfect and forgets the quarrels.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 6B, Thursday.

Darshan joined us from a school in Surat three weeks ago. He often says, "At my old school, everyone was nice. We never had fights." Today he said it after a small quarrel over a cricket ball with Vijay.

I asked him gently, "Never any fights at all?" He thought and said, "Well... once a boy broke my kite." Then he smiled a little.

I think Darshan misses his friends and the old school feels perfect from far away. I've paired him with Vijay for the science project, and I'll check in with him again next week.

qa.q: Who did Darshan quarrel with over a cricket ball?
qa.a: Vijay.

qa.q: Why might Darshan say everyone at his old school was nice?
qa.a: He probably feels lonely and misses his friends, so the old school seems perfect and the fights have faded.

qa.q: What did the teacher do to help Darshan settle in?
qa.a: The teacher paired him with Vijay for the science project and plans to check in next week.

qa.q: How might Vijay feel hearing that Darshan's old school never had fights?
qa.a: Vijay might feel a bit hurt or annoyed, as if he's being compared unfairly.

grounding: A teacher notes a child who has moved schools remembering the old class as perfect and forgetting the quarrels.

passage:
Sunday

I miss my old school in Pune SO much. We had the big mango tree and we played kho-kho every break. Everyone liked me.

Here in Nagpur it's hot, and the kids already have best friends.

But today I found my old diary from last year. It said: "Chaitanya and Meenal didn't let me play. I sat alone at the mango tree." And another page: "I hate kho-kho, I always get out first."

I don't remember that at all!! I only remember the good things.

Maybe new school will be okay later. Old school wasn't only good.

— Chandrika

qa.q: What did Chandrika play every break at the old school?
qa.a: Kho-kho.

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel reading the old diary?
qa.a: Chandrika felt surprised and a little confused, since those bad days had been forgotten.

qa.q: What small step might help Chandrika at the new school?
qa.a: Chandrika could try joining one game at break, remembering that the old school also took time to feel good.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya have seen things at the old school?
qa.a: Chaitanya might not even remember leaving Chandrika out, since it probably felt small at the time.

grounding: A child who moved schools remembers the old one as perfect until an old diary shows the quarrels.

passage: On the first Onam since the family moved to the kasba, Devika sat on the verandah making a small pookalam and sighing. "In my old school everyone was kind," she told her older brother Gautam. "We never fought. Not once." Gautam raised an eyebrow. "Remember when a girl in your row tore your notebook and you cried all the way home? And the boys who wouldn't let you play kho-kho?" Devika frowned at her petals. She did remember, a little, now that he said it. But in her mind the old classroom was sunny and full of laughter, and the new one was loud and strange. "Still," she said, "it was better." Gautam smiled and handed her a yellow flower.

passage: During Meskel week, Abebe's family lit a small bonfire in the yard of their new flat in Nairobi. Abebe watched the sparks and thought of his old school in Addis Ababa. "My old class was the best in the world," he told Fatima, the girl from next door who had come to watch. "Everyone shared their injera. Nobody ever got in trouble." Fatima tilted her head. "Nobody? Ever?" Abebe thought of the boy who used to hide his shoes, and the teacher who made him stand outside for talking. Those days felt far away and soft, like the fire's glow. "Almost nobody," he said. Fatima grinned. "My class hides shoes too. You could join our football game tomorrow."

qa.q: Where was Abebe's old school?
qa.a: In Addis Ababa.

qa.q: Why does Abebe say his old class was the best in the world?
qa.a: He misses home and feels a bit lonely in Nairobi, so distance makes the old class seem perfect; the shoe-hiding and being sent outside feel far away and soft.

qa.q: What small step from Fatima helps?
qa.a: Inviting him to tomorrow's football game gives him a way into the new place instead of only looking back.

qa.q: How might Fatima see Abebe's story about the best class?
qa.a: She finds it a bit too perfect but understands, and connects by saying her class hides shoes too.

grounding: A boy who moved away remembers his old class as perfect, forgetting the quarrels, during a festival in his new home.

passage: At the summer holiday camp in her new school, Gopika sat apart during craft hour. The camp counsellor knelt beside her. "Missing your old school?" "It was perfect there," Gopika said. "Everyone liked me. We never argued." A boy at the next table, Hrithik, looked up; he had moved from the same old school a year earlier. "Gopika, remember the class monitor fight? You didn't talk to anyone for a week." Gopika's cheeks went warm. She did remember, now. It seemed small and far away, like a faded picture. "That was only once," she muttered. The counsellor smiled. "Old places get prettier when we miss them. Want to make a card for someone new here?"

qa.q: What was Gopika doing during craft hour?
qa.a: Sitting apart.

qa.q: What did Gopika feel when Hrithik mentioned the monitor fight?
qa.a: Her cheeks went warm; she felt embarrassed and a bit defensive, because it didn't fit her perfect picture of the old school.

qa.q: How did the counsellor help, and what could come next?
qa.a: By saying old places get prettier when we miss them, and inviting her to make a card for someone new, a small step toward the present.

qa.q: What is it like for Hrithik to hear Gopika's version?
qa.a: He remembers the real quarrels, so he may feel he should be honest, and perhaps a bit amused.

grounding: A girl new to a school remembers her old class as perfect, forgetting the quarrels a former classmate recalls.

passage:
Monday, first week after the monsoon break. At his new school in Nagpur, Pranav sat alone at lunch. At home he told Harish Chacha, "My old class was perfect. Everyone was my friend. We never fought."
Thursday. Harish Chacha found Pranav's old notebook while unpacking a box. Inside the back cover, in angry pencil: "Rohan and Arjun left me out AGAIN. I hate this class." Pranav read it and frowned. "I don't remember that."
Saturday. A boy from his new class, Dev, knocked with a cricket bat. Pranav hesitated at the door. "My old friends were better," he muttered. Then he looked at the notebook on the table, picked up his cap, and went out to play.

qa.q: What was written inside the back cover of Pranav's old notebook?
qa.a: "Rohan and Arjun left me out AGAIN. I hate this class."

qa.q: Why does Pranav remember his old class as perfect?
qa.a: He feels lonely at the new school, and distance has smoothed away the quarrels, so the old class feels warm and flawless.

qa.q: How could Harish Chacha help Pranav settle in?
qa.a: He could gently remind Pranav that the old class had hard days too, and encourage small chances like Dev's cricket game.

qa.q: What might Dev think if Pranav had refused to come out?
qa.a: Dev might have felt rejected and stopped knocking, never knowing Pranav was comparing him with a class that only seemed perfect.

grounding: Shows a child who moved schools remembering the old class as perfect and forgetting its quarrels.
